Across all three 50 segment-specific phylogenies, the outbreak virus clustered within an ANDV Clade III 51 cluster spanning southern Chile and northern Patagonia in Argentina and were most closely 52 related to a human-derived ANDV (p1236) collected in Los Ríos Region of Chile in 2012, 53 representing the closest known historical relative of the outbreak-associated virus. 54 Phylogeographic analysis showed that the genetically distinct ANDV Clade V lineage 55 circulating in central Chile was not closely related to the cruise ship outbreak-associated 56 genomes, thereby reducing the likelihood that the index cases acquired infection through 57 zoonotic spillover while traveling through the Maule Region. Recent genomic and epidemiological 66 investigations characterized the outbreak variant and reconstructed key elements of the 67 travel history of the presumed index cases1. However, the precise geographic site and 68 circumstances of the initial zoonotic spillover remain unresolved. 69 Andes virus (ANDV) is a rodent-borne orthohantavirus in subfamily Mammantavirinae of 70 family Hantaviridae. It is classified within the species Orthohantavirus andesense together 71 with three closely related “ANDV-like” viruses, Castelo dos Sonhos virus (CASV), 72 Lechiguanas virus (LECV), and Orán virus (ORNV). Like all orthohantaviruses, ANDV 73 has a trisegmented negative-sense RNA genome2. 74 Genomic analysis identified the cruise ship outbreak agent as ANDV and showed that the 75 outbreak-associated genome sequences were most closely related to ANDV genome 76 sequences causing HPS cases in Province of Neuquén, Argentina3,4. In particular, the cruise 77 ship outbreak virus genome sequence clustered with sequences from HPS cases in Villa 78 Meliquina, San Martín de los Andes, and Villa Traful, documented between 2017 and 79 20264. Pairwise comparisons showed approximately 98.7% nucleotide identity between the 80 cruise-associated virus sequence and the closest Province of Neuquén small (S), medium 81 (M), and large (L) genome segment sequences4. The cruise variant reference sequence, 82 ANDV-Switzerland-Hu-3337-2026, differs from the NRC4/2018 Province of Neuquén 83 reference sequence by 23 single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in the S, 47 in the M, and 84 in 84 the L segment. Most mutations were synonymous; nonsynonymous mutations were 85 predicted to result in V70I and K144R changes in the large (L) protein (encoded by the L 86 segment), and T193A, T516I, and A994T changes in glycoprotein precursor (GPC; 87 encoded by the M segment)3,5. These genome sequences from Province of Neuquén were 88 interpreted3,4 as the closest sampled human representatives of a broader ANDV population 89 circulating across northern Patagonia in Argentina and southern Chile. However, they are 90 not sufficiently closely related to be considered direct ancestors of the cruise ship outbreak- 91 associated virus. 92 Closely related rodent-derived sequences were recently made available6. In a pairwise 93 comparison against the Swiss cruise-ship reference genome sequence 94 ANDV/Switzerland/Hu-3337/2026 (PZ385161.1, PZ385162.1, and PZ385163.1)7, the 95 closest rodent-derived ANDV sequence from Chile in the available set, R175, still differs 96 by 68 unambiguous nucleotide substitutions across the three segments: 36 SNVs in L, 23 in 97 M, and 9 in S. This level of divergence is still substantially greater than that reported by 98 Kim et al.8, who used active targeted surveillance to identify the geographical site of 99 Hantaan virus emergence. In their study, paired human and rodent Hantaan virus sequences 100 differed by only 8–30 nucleotide substitutions across the complete trisegmented genome, 101 depending on the human–rodent pair. Thus, the currently available rodent sequences from 102 Chile should be interpreted as evidence of broader unsampled regional diversity rather than 103 as the likely immediate source. 104 Our epidemiological reconstruction showed that the presumed index cases, Cases 1 and 2, 105 travelled extensively by motorhome through Argentina, Uruguay and Chile before 106 embarking on the cruise in Ushuaia, Province of Tierra del Fuego, Antarctica and South 107 Atlantic Islands, Argentina, on 1 April 2026. This work will focus on their travel through 108 Chile. They entered Chile’s Aysén Region on 9 January, returning to Argentina via the 109 Icalma Pass on 31 January. These regions are known for the circulation of ANDV and the 110 presence of long-tailed colilargos (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus (Bennett, 1832)), ANDV’s 111 main spillover rodent reservoirs9. On 12 February, Cases 1 and 2 moved via the Pehuenche 112 Pass to Maule Region in Chile, and re-entered Argentina four days later via the same pass 113 (Figure 3). 114 Recently generated complete genome sequence data from human-derived ANDV in Chile, 115 spanning a period between 2011–202410, now provides an opportunity to evaluate this 116 possibility in a higher-resolution phylogeographic framework. That dataset defines 117 geographically structured ANDV diversity in Chile, including a new northern/central 118 lineage (ANDV Chi-North, from now on referred to as ANDV Clade V). In the present 119 study, we expanded this framework by incorporating additional 2025–2026 sequences from 120 Chile together with HPS outbreak-associated ANDV genomes. By comparing the cruise 121 ship outbreak variant sequence with this expanded dataset and by mapping those 122 relationships against the reconstructed travel itinerary of the index cases, we evaluate 123 whether the initial zoonotic ANDV spillover could have occurred in Chile or in an 124 unsampled cross-border extension of the northern Patagonia from Argentina. 125 Results 126 Cruise ship outbreak-associated Andes virus genome sequences cluster with those of 127 Andes viruses circulating in the Hua Hum Pass corridor 128 To better understand the ancestry of the cruise ship-associated ANDV, we leveraged three 129 sequence datasets populated exclusively with complete genome sequences comprising the 130 ANDV S, M, and L segments: cruise ship outbreak-associated ANDV, Argentina-endemic 131 ANDV, and Chile-endemic ANDV genome sequences. This complete genome sequence 132 approach was adopted to minimize biases arising from segment-specific phylogenetic 133 discordance and to enable direct comparison across the S, M, and L segments. Maximum- 134 likelihood phylogenetic analyses placed each cruise ship outbreak-associated genome 135 segment sequence within previously described ANDV diversity, clustering with sequences 136 belonging to ANDV Clade III2, in a distinct cluster, here designated “Hua Hum Pass 137 corridor (HHPC)”, composed predominantly of historical human-derived ANDV genome 138 sequences from La Araucanía and Los Ríos Regions in Chile together with related northern 139 Patagonian sequences from Argentina (Fig. 1). 140 Within the S segment phylogeny (Fig. 1a), cruise ship outbreak-associated genome 141 sequences clustered with sequences derived from Chile p1236 (Los Ríos Region, 2012), 142 p931 (Los Ríos Region, 2020), p1242 (Los Ríos Region, 2013), p1239 (Los Ríos Region, 143 2013), p132D (Los Ríos Region, 2026), and p1059 (La Araucanía Region, 2023), together 144 with Argentinian Province of Neuquén genome sequences NRC-3/18 and NRC-4/18. 145 Similar clustering patterns were observed independently in the M (Fig. 1b) and L (Fig. 1c) 146 segment phylogeny. 147 Within the HHPC cluster, p1236 emerged as the closest sampled human-derived relative of 148 the cruise ship outbreak-associated viruses across all three genome segments. The patient 149 was a 7-year-old male from the Lanco commune (Los Ríos Region, southern Chile) who 150 experienced symptom onset on November 7, 2012. Epidemiologically, his infection was an 151 isolated incident linked to rural exposure, with no associated cluster or secondary cases. He 152 sought treatment at the hospital in Panguipulli, where his condition deteriorated into a 153 severe presentation of HPS. Because ECMO was unavailable at that specific facility, his 154 critical respiratory failure was managed with invasive mechanical ventilation. This life- 155 saving intervention firmly aligns his illness with the study's "severe" clinical classification. 156 Despite the critical, life-threatening nature of the disease, the child successfully survived 157 and was discharged on November 22, 2012. Although the complete L segment could not be 158 recovered for p1236, the available partial L sequence contained two unresolved regions at 159 positions 4008–5185 and 5461–6562. Nevertheless, the available L-segment regions 160 supported the same phylogenetic placement observed for the S and M segments. In each 161 segment-specific phylogeny, p1236 is positioned more closely to the cruise ship outbreak 162 genome sequences than NRC-4/2018, which had previously represented the closest 163 available complete human-derived comparator3,4. Direct comparison between p1236 and 164 the Swiss outbreak-associated case revealed 18 nucleotide differences in the S segment, 165 with no nonsynonymous substitutions; 28 nucleotide differences in the M segment, 166 including two nonsynonymous substitutions; and 78 nucleotide differences across the 167 4,535-nt available portion of the L segment, including three nonsynonymous substitutions. 168 Although overall similarity levels remained comparable, these findings substantially refine 169 the genomic context of the cruise ship outbreak-associated variant by linking it to a 170 historical human-derived ANDV detected in southern Chile rather than exclusively to 171 northern Patagonian genome sequences from Argentina. 172 Bayesian phylogenetic analyses recovered highly consistent maximum clade credibility 173 (MCC) trees, corroborating the phylogenetic placement inferred by maximum-likelihood 174 analyses (Supplementary Figure S1). 175 Motivated by published evidence suggesting potential reassortment including the 176 phylogenetic placement of the publicly available rodent-derived genome R600 from the 177 Los Ríos Region of Chile (2013), which clustered with the outbreak-associated genomes in 178 the L-segment phylogeny but not in the S and M phylogenies7, we performed a 179 comprehensive reassortment analysis across our complete dataset. This analysis detected no 180 evidence of reassortment among Clade III genomes (Supplementary Figure S2), 181 supporting the interpretation that the HHPC cluster represents a single evolutionary lineage. 182 Several additional human-associated genome sequences composing the HHPC cluster were 183 obtained from HPS cases identified since 2012 in southern Chile. These cases included 184 sporadic infections, epidemiologically linked clusters, and a range of clinical outcomes 185 (Supplementary Table S1). Together, these findings indicate that the HHPC cluster 186 represents a long-standing component of ANDV diversity in southern Chile and northern 187 Patagonia in Argentina. 188 The Hua Hum Pass corridor Andes virus cluster is defined by limited, largely neutral 189 molecular signatures within Andes virus Clade III diversity 190 No major genomic insertions, deletions, or segment-specific genomic features distinguished 191 HHPC cluster genome sequences from those of other ANDV Clade III members. 192 Comparison of deduced amino acid variation identified a limited number of 193 phylogenetically informative substitutions. Consistent with previous analyses10, ANDV 194 Clade III was characterized by substitutions including GPC I114V, A193T and V1127I. 195 Within this genetic background, genomes composing the HHPC cluster consistently 196 encoded GPC T1055, whereas the remaining analyzed ANDV Clade III genomes encoded 197 GPC A1055. Additional cluster-enriched changes included nucleoprotein (S segment) 198 substitution L7I and L protein (L segment) R144K and A541V. Together, these 199 substitutions define a molecular signature that distinguishes the HHPC cluster within the 200 broader diversity of ANDV Clade III (Supplementary Table S2). A comprehensive 201 comparison of all deduced amino acid substitutions identified among HHPC cluster 202 genome sequences relative to the five recognized ANDV clades (Clades I–V) and 203 representative orthohantaviruses is provided in Supplementary Table S3. 204 Previously proposed amino acid markers associated with person-to-person transmission in 205 Argentinian HPS outbreaks11 were not consistently encoded in HHPC cluster genome 206 sequences. The only substitution unique to the cruise ship outbreak lineage was GPC 207 T516I, which remained exclusive after inclusion of the expanded genomic dataset from 208 Chile. In the absence of structural or comparative evidence supporting an effect on 209 glycoprotein stability or function, T516I is best interpreted as a molecular marker of the 210 common-source outbreak, potentially reflecting stochastic drift in the local reservoir 211 population. Its phenotypic relevance will require direct functional testing in virion-like 212 particle (VLP) or pseudotype systems. 213 Structural mapping of HHPC cluster-associated SNV-encoded amino acid residue changes 214 onto GPC-encoded GN/Gc showed that three of the five substitutions are located in surface- 215 exposed regions of the spikes, whereas the remaining two are located within the GN 216 endodomain and GC transmembrane (Supplementary Figure S3). Although the surface- 217 exposed substitutions could be compatible with immune-driven selection, none overlapped 218 with previously reported neutralizing antibody epitopes or escape variants. Similarly, the 219 three L protein-associated substitutions mapped outside of the known catalytic sites of this 220 multifunctional protein12 (Supplementary Figure S4). The potential structural impact was 221 further analyzed with deep learning-based tools, which indicated only minor changes in 222 Gibbs free energy (ΔΔG) values, suggesting that these variants are unlikely to substantially 223 affect protein stability or quaternary assembly. analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒(ANDV)在2026年导致一次跨国汉坦病毒肺综合征暴发,感染对象为一艘邮轮的乘客和船员。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究对来自智利的完整ANDV小(S)、中(M)和大(L)基因组片段序列,以及与暴发相关的和公开可得的序列,采用系统发育方法进行分析。

papers.title: Bile acid signaling at the gut–vascular interface: a novel modulator of hantavirus endothelial barrier dysfunction
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infection triggers life-threatening hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), driven by severe endothelial barrier breakdown and systemic capillary leakage. Clinical severity varies widely with undefined host regulators, and no targeted endothelial-protective treatments exist. Recent data link hantaviruses to gut microbiome remodeling, while bile acid (BA) receptors FXR and TGR5 potently inhibit NF-κB-mediated endothelial inflammation. We synthesize four core lines of evidence. First, metagenomic reports confirm hantavirus reshapes gut/lung microbiota in rodent reservoirs. Second, we re-analyzed three public GEO datasets via standardized RNA-seq/microarray pipelines: (i) GSE245916: SEOV-infected human/rat lung ECs show conserved VCAM1/ICAM1 upregulation (human VCAM1 log 2 FC=+1.17, P = 0.023; rat Icam1 log 2 FC=+0.32, padj=0.016) with unaltered FXR; (ii) GSE7271: SEOV-infected rat lung displays sustained Nfkb1 suppression (all timepoints, P<0.05) and day-15 Slc10a2 downregulation (P = 0.028); (iii) GSE270172: PUUV 3D vessel chips feature robust IL6 elevation (log 2 FC=+1.22, P = 3.1×10 -8 ) and disrupted BA transporters (ABCC3 log 2 FC=−1.44, P = 7.4×10 - 12). TGR5 (GPBAR1) was undetectable in endothelial cells across all datasets. Third, FXR/TGR5 agonists repress NF-κB inflammation and mitigate lung vascular injury. Fourth, HTNV upregulates CH25H to block HMGCR-dependent cholesterol synthesis, depleting BA precursor substrates. We propose a unified pathogenic model: hantavirus-triggered gut dysbiosis plus virus-impaired cholesterol metabolism deplete circulating FXR/TGR5 agonistic BAs, relieving constitutive inhibition of endothelial NF-κB and monocyte NLRP3 inflammasomes to exacerbate capillary leakage. We define tiered testable predictions covering clinical multi-omics cohorts, in vitro receptor modulation assays and in vivo pharmacological interventions. This gut microbiota–BA–FXR/TGR5 axis represents a repurposable therapeutic target for hantavirus diseases, though direct causal evidence connecting BA signaling to viral vascular damage remains absent; our framework offers a rigorous testable roadmap for subsequent validation.
papers.journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology

The pathological hallmark of hantavirus disease is not direct viral cytolysis, but rather a profound functional disruption of the microvascular endothelial barrier. Monocyte-derived TNF-a, IL-1b, and IL-6 are secreted upon hantavirus sensing and act in a paracrine manner to increase endothelial permeability, an effect that is reversed by anti-TNF-a neutralizing antibody (Wang et al., 2026). IL-6 trans-signaling directly disrupts VE-cadherin organization and correlates with disease severity in HFRS patients [Maleki et al., 2025]. Soluble thrombomodulin (sTM) has been validated as a biomarker that tracks disease progression and predicts mortality in HFRS (Wei et al., 2026). At the transcriptional level, NF-kB-driven cytokine storm is recognized as the shared core pathology across the Bunyaviricetes class (Casel et al., 2026). A fundamental and clinically consequential question remains unresolved: why do some patients infected with the same hantavirus strain develop fulminant, life-threatening capillary leak while others experience mild or subclinical illness? Host genetic factors, includ- ing HLA haplotypes and CCR5 polymorphisms, explain only a fraction of the observed variability (Kletenkov et al., 2019; Haapaniemi et al., 2025). Viral factors such as inoculum dose and strain also contribute, but do not fully account for the severity spectrum. Notably, the literature lacks a comprehensive framework integrating microbial, metabolic, and immunological determinants of hantavirus disease severity. Addressing this gap, we propose a novel hypothesis linking the gut microbiota–bile acid axis, mediated by the Farnesoid X receptor (FXR, NR1H4) and Takeda G protein- coupled receptor 5 (TGR5, GPBAR1), to endothelial barrier dys- function. Importantly, no clinical metagenomic or metabolomic data from HFRS patients are currently available to test this hypothesis; the present article provides the conceptual framework and specific experimental predictions required to generate such data. The gut–lung axis—the bidirectional immunological and met- abolic crosstalk between the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts mediated by the gut microbiome and its metabolites—has emerged as a critical determinant of severity in multiple viral respiratory diseases, including influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and respiratory syncy- tial virus (Budden et al., 2017; Özçam and Lynch, 2024). This axis operates through multiple interconnected mechanisms: (1) micro- bial metabolites, particularly short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and secondary bile acids (BAs), enter the portal and systemic circula- tions to modulate pulmonary immune tone through G-protein- coupled receptors (e.g., GPR41/43 for SCFAs, TGR5 for BAs) and nuclear receptors (e.g., FXR) (Zhang et al., 2012; Özçam and Lynch, 2024); (2) gut-derived cytokines and immune cells traffic through the lymphatic and circulatory systems to influence lung mucosal immunity; (3) dietary and microbial metabolites such as tryptophan derivatives activate aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) signaling in lung epithelial and immune cells (Özçam and Lynch, 2024). Importantly, gut microbiota dysbiosis—characterized by reduced microbial diversity and altered BA-metabolizing capacity—can shift the systemic BA pool composition, decreasing FXR/TGR5 agonistic profiles and consequently amplifying pulmonary inflammatory responses (Zhang et al., 2012; Ridlon et al., 2016). Bile acids, in particular, represent a direct metabolic link between gut microbial ecology and remote vascular barrier function, as they are exclusively produced in the liver, modified by the gut microbiota, and delivered via the circulation to peripheral tissues including the lung and kidney capillaries (Özçam and Lynch, 2024). Despite the extensive characterization of the gut–lung axis in other viral infections, this axis remains entirely unexplored in the context of hantavirus disease. A PubMed search for (“hantavirus” OR “HFRS”) AND (“bile acid” OR “FXR” OR “TGR5” OR “NR1H4” OR “GPBAR1”) returns zero results (as of May 2026). Notably, serum BA profiles have emerged as biomarkers of disease severity and gut barrier dysfunction in other viral infections: elevated total BA and altered BA composition predict poor outcomes in COVID-19, and BA dysregulation has been linked to intestinal permeability and sys- temic inflammation in influenza and hepatitis (Özçam and Lynch, 2024).Complementarily, severe pulmonary inflammatory insults— including viral-induced endothelial injury—can circulate systemic pro-inflammatory signals back to the gastrointestinal tract, disrupt- ing intestinal barrier integrity and reshaping bile acid-metabolizing commensal populations, thereby forming a self-amplifying inflam- matory feedback loop. This uncharted intersection between bile acid gut–lung signaling and hantavirus-triggered pulmonary endo- thelial dysfunction constitutes the core mechanistic basis of our gut–vascular interface hypothesis proposed herein. We use the term “gut–vascular interface” (GVI) to denote the systemic signaling axis through which microbiota-derived bile acid metabolites reach and modulate the function of distal microvascular endothelial beds—including those of the kidney and, in severe cases, Liu et al. 10.3389/fcimb.2026.1883162 Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology frontiersin.org 02 the lung—the principal target organs in hantavirus disease. This concept is built upon the established gut–vascular barrier (GVB), first identified in the small intestine by Spadoni et al (Spadoni et al., 2015). The GVB comprises intestinal endothelial cells intercon- nected by tight junctions (occludin, ZO-1, cingulin, JAM-A) and adherens junctions (VE-cadherin, b-catenin), stabilized by enteric glial cells and pericytes, and restricts the passage of solutes and macromolecules above approximately 70 kDa into the bloodstream (Spadoni et al., 2015). The integrity of this barrier is maintained by the canonical Wnt/b-catenin signaling pathway, and its disruption —marked by upregulation of the endothelial glycoprotein plasma- lemma vesicle-associated protein-1 (PV-1)—has been shown to facilitate bacterial translocation from the gut to distant organs, including the liver (Bertocchi et al., 2021). GVB disruption further triggers systemic innate immune activation: translocated microbial fragments and aberrant circulating BA profiles jointly stimulate tissue-resident macrophages at pulmonary and renal microvascular beds, driving local NF-kB-dependent pro-inflammatory cytokine release and amplifying endothelial barrier leakage—the core path- ological phenotype of hantavirus-induced HFRS. Beyond its barrier function, the GVI serves as an endocrine-like conduit for bile acids (BAs), which are synthesized in the liver, conjugated with taurine or glycine, secreted into the duodenum, deconjugated and modified by the gut microbiota, and then reabsorbed via the portal circulation to reach systemic endothelial beds. The composition of the recirculating BA pool is therefore directly shaped by gut microbial ecology, linking intestinal dysbiosis to remote vascular sites. This concept is mechanistically distinct from the traditional “gut–lung axis” mucosal immunity framework, though the two are comple- mentary. While the gut–lung axis emphasizes local immune cell trafficking, IgA-mediated mucosal defense, and direct microbial metabolite effects on respiratory epithelium, the GVI focuses on the endocrine-like delivery of BA receptor ligands via the portal and systemic circulation to endothelial and immune cells at remote vascular sites. We employ this terminology throughout the manu- script to distinguish the systemic BA-farnesoid X receptor (FXR, NR1H4)/G protein-coupled bile acid receptor 1 (TGR5, GPBAR1) signaling paradigm from mucosal immune cross-talk.The anatom- ical and functional components of the GVI are schematically illustrated in Supplementary Figure 1. Bile acids signal through two major receptor systems with established roles in vascular inflammation and endothelial barrier maintenance. Farnesoid X receptor (FXR, NR1H4), a nuclear receptor expressed at low levels in endothelial cells, functionally antagonizes NF-kB p65 transcriptional activity through co-repressor recruitment (Zhang et al., 2012), suppressing expression of VCAM1, ICAM1, TNF, and IL6. Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5, GPBAR1), expressed predominantly in monocytes and macrophages but below detection in quiescent endothelial cells (Perino and Schoonjans, 2015), signals through cAMP/PKA to inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation and suppress TNF-a, IL-6, and IL-1b secretion (Hu et al., 2021). Both receptors are activated by bile acids: CDCA is the most potent endogenous FXR agonist, while secondary bile acids LCA and DCA are TGR5 agonists. The compo- sition of the BA pool is directly determined by gut microbial metabolism, with bile salt hydrolase (BSH)-active bacteria serving as gatekeepers of BA receptor signaling (Ridlon et al., 2016). Elevated intestinal BA concentrations secondary to dysbiosis may directly impair barrier integrity and exacerbate systemic inflammation (Ridlon et al., 2016), reinforcing the gut–vascular axis concept.The signaling cascades of both receptors downstream of bile acid activa- tion are schematically summarized in Supplementary Figure 2. The objective of this hypothesis article is to integrate dispersed published evidence across metagenomics, transcriptomics, BA re- ceptor pharmacology, and cholesterol metabolism to construct a testable framework linking bile acid signaling to hantavirus endo- thelial pathology—a connection that has not been previously proposed. Here, we synthesize four converging evidence chains to propose that the gut microbiota–bile acid–FXR/TGR5 axis func- tions as a host-intrinsic modulator of endothelial barrier integrity in hantavirus disease. We propose that hantavirus-induced microbiome perturbation, combined with virus-mediated disrup- tion of cholesterol metabolism, shifts the bile acid pool away from FXR/TGR5-agonistic profiles, reducing tonic suppression of endo- thelial NF-kB signaling and thereby potentially amplifying vascular leakage. We outline specific, testable predictions. We emphasize that direct evidence linking BA signaling to hantavirus pathogenesis currently does not exist; this article provides a testable framework for investigation. Evidence supporting the gut microbiota–bile acid–FXR/TGR5 axis hypothesis Until recently, the effect of hantavirus infection on host-asso- ciated microbial communities was entirely unknown. Two land- mark studies have now established that hantaviruses may directly alter the composition of both gut and lung microbiomes in their natural rodent reservoirs, providing the foundational evidence for the first link in our hypothesis. The first direct evidence emerged from a study of wild bank voles (Myodes glareolus), the natural reservoir host of PUUV. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing of intestinal samples, the authors demonstrated that PUUV infection significantly altered both a- diversity (increased) and b-diversity of the gut microbiota, with pathogen-specific community patterns that distinguished PUUV- monoinfected animals from those co-infected with other rodent pathogens. These alterations were not attributable to host age, sex, or body condition, suggesting a virus-specific effect on gut microbial community structure (Brila et al., 2023). Direct experimental evidence that hantavirus can infect and disrupt the gastrointestinal epithelium was provided by Witkowski et al. full_text_sections.full_text: Bile acid signaling at the gut–vascular interface: a novel modulator of hantavirus endothelial barrier dysfunction Lei Liu 1*, Jiyong Lin 2, Kai Sang 1, Jianping Lai 1, Na Huang 1, Peiling Zhong 1, Yuxiang Liu 2* and Sheng Chen 3* 1Department of Infectious Diseases, Shenzhen Traditional Chinese Medicine Hospital, The Fourth Clinical Medical College of Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine, Shenzhen, China, 2Department of Emergency, Shenzhen Traditional Chinese Medicine Hospital, The Fourth Clinical Medical College of Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine, Shenzhen, China, 3Department of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, Shenzhen Traditional Chinese Medicine Hospital, The Fourth Clinical Medical College of Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine, Shenzhen, China Hantavirus infection triggers life-threatening hemorrhagic fever with renal syn- drome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), driven by severe endothelial barrier breakdown and systemic capillary leakage. Clinical severity varies widely with undefined host regulators, and no targeted endothe- lial-protective treatments exist. Recent data link hantaviruses to gut microbiome remodeling, while bile acid (BA) receptors FXR and TGR5 potently inhibit NF-kB- mediated endothelial inflammation. We synthesize four core lines of evidence. First, metagenomic reports confirm hantavirus reshapes gut/lung microbiota in rodent reservoirs. Second, we re-analyzed three public GEO datasets via stan- dardized RNA-seq/microarray pipelines: (i) GSE245916: SEOV-infected human/ rat lung ECs show conserved VCAM1/ICAM1 upregulation (human VCAM1 log2FC=+1.17, P = 0.023; rat Icam1 log2FC=+0.32, padj=0.016) with unaltered FXR; (ii) GSE7271: SEOV-infected rat lung displays sustained Nfkb1 suppression (all timepoints, P<0.05) and day-15 Slc10a2 downregulation (P = 0.028); (iii) GSE270172: PUUV 3D vessel chips feature robust IL6 elevation (log2FC= +1.22, P = 3.1×10-8) and disrupted BA transporters (ABCC3 log2FC=−1.44, P = 7.4×10-12). TGR5 (GPBAR1) was undetectable in endothelial cells across all datasets. Third, FXR/TGR5 agonists repress NF-kB inflammation and mitigate lung vascular injury. Fourth, HTNV upregulates CH25H to block HMGCR-dependent cholesterol synthesis, depleting BA precursor substrates. We propose a unified pathogenic model: hantavirus-triggered gut dysbiosis plus virus-impaired cho- lesterol metabolism deplete circulating FXR/TGR5 agonistic BAs, relieving con- stitutive inhibition of endothelial NF-kB and monocyte NLRP3 inflammasomes to exacerbate capillary leakage. We define tiered testable predictions covering clinical multi-omics cohorts, in vitro receptor modulation assays and in vivo pharmacological interventions. This gut microbiota–BA–FXR/TGR5 axis repre- sents a repurposable therapeutic target for hantavirus diseases, though direct causal evidence connecting BA signaling to viral vascular damage remains absent; our framework offers a rigorous testable roadmap for subsequent validation. analysis.background: Hantavirus infection causes life‑threatening HFRS and HCPS by inducing severe endothelial barrier breakdown and systemic capillary leakage (A1). Clinical severity is highly variable and no endothelial‑protective therapies exist (A2). Recent work links hantavirus infection to gut microbiome remodeling and shows that bile‑acid receptors FXR and TGR5 can inhibit NF‑κB‑driven endothelial inflammation (A3).
analysis.methods: The authors synthesized four lines of evidence: (i) metagenomic reports of hantavirus‑induced gut/lung microbiota changes in rodent reservoirs (A5); (ii) re‑analysis of three public GEO datasets (GSE245916, GSE7271, GSE270172) using standardized RNA‑seq/microarray pipelines to assess endothelial gene expression (A6‑A10); (iii) literature on FXR/TGR5 agonists suppressing NF‑κB inflammation and reducing lung vascular injury (A11); and (iv) reports that HTNV up‑regulates CH25H, impairing cholesterol‑derived bile‑acid precursors (A12).
analysis.results: Re‑analysis showed conserved up‑regulation of VCAM1 (human log2FC +1.17, P = 0.023) and ICAM1 (rat log2FC +0.32, padj = 0.016) without FXR change (A6‑A7); sustained Nfkb1 suppression and Slc10a2 down‑regulation (P = 0.028) in infected rat lung (A8); strong IL6 elevation (log2FC +1.22, P = 3.1×10⁻⁸) and loss of BA transporter ABCC3 (log2FC −1.44, P = 7.4×10⁻¹²) in PUUV‑infected vessel chips (A9); TGR5 was undetectable in endothelial cells (A10). FXR/TGR5 agonists reduced NF‑κB activity and mitigated vascular injury (A11), and HTNV‑induced CH25H up‑regulation blocked HMGCR‑dependent cholesterol synthesis (A12).
analysis.contribution: The paper proposes a unified pathogenic model linking hantavirus‑driven gut dysbiosis and impaired cholesterol metabolism to depletion of FXR/TGR5 agonistic bile acids, thereby releasing inhibition of endothelial NF‑κB and monocyte NLRP3 inflammasomes (A13). It outlines tiered, testable predictions for multi‑omics clinical cohorts, in‑vitro receptor assays, and in‑vivo pharmacologic interventions (A14). The gut‑microbiota–bile‑acid–FXR/TGR5 axis is highlighted as a repurposable therapeutic target for hantavirus disease (A15).
analysis.limitations: The authors acknowledge that direct causal evidence linking bile‑acid signaling to hantavirus‑induced vascular damage is absent (A15); the work is a hypothesis‑driven synthesis relying on re‑analysis of existing datasets rather than new experimental data.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus causes severe HFRS/HCPS via endothelial barrier breakdown, with variable severity and no targeted treatments; gut microbiome changes and bile‑acid receptors FXR/TGR5 can modulate inflammation (A1‑A3). Methods: The study synthesizes metagenomic reports, re‑analyzes three GEO datasets (GSE245916, GSE7271, GSE270172) for endothelial gene expression, reviews FXR/TGR5 agonist effects, and examines HTNV‑induced CH25H up‑regulation (A5‑A12). Results: VCAM1/ICAM1 are up‑regulated (human log2FC +1.17, P = 0.023; rat log2FC +0.32, padj = 0.016), Nfkb1 is suppressed, Slc10a2 down‑regulated (P = 0.028), IL6 elevated (log2FC +1.22, P = 3.1×10⁻⁸), BA transporter ABCC3 reduced (log2FC −1.44, P = 7.4×10⁻¹²), TGR5 absent, and FXR/TGR5 agonists mitigate NF‑κB inflammation (A6‑A12). Contribution: Proposes a model where gut dysbiosis and cholesterol‑metabolism disruption deplete FXR/TGR5 agonistic bile acids, enhancing NF‑κB/NLRP3 activity, and suggests this axis as a therapeutic target with testable predictions (A13‑A15). Limitations: No direct causal evidence is provided; conclusions are based on re‑analysis and hypothesis rather than new experimental data (A15).

papers.title_zh: 肠道-血管界面的胆汁酸信号:调节汉坦病毒内皮屏障功能障碍的新型因子

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 感染通过诱导严重的内皮屏障破坏和全身毛细血管渗漏导致危及生命的肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征 (A1)。临床严重程度差异很大,且目前没有内皮保护疗法 (A2)。最新研究将 汉坦病毒 感染与肠道微生物组重塑关联,并显示胆汁酸受体 FXR 和 TGR5 能抑制 NF-κB 介导的内皮炎症 (A3)。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者综合了四条证据:(i) 来自啮齿动物宿主的 汉坦病毒 引起的肠道/肺部微生物群变化的宏基因组报告 (A5);(ii) 使用标准化 RNA‐seq/微阵列流程对三个公开 GEO 数据集 (GSE245916, GSE7271, GSE270172) 进行重新分析,以评估内皮基因表达 (A6‐A10);(iii) 有关 FXR/TGR5 激动剂抑制 NF‐κB 炎症并减轻肺血管损伤的文献 (A11);以及 (iv) 报告 HTNV 上调 CH25H,损害胆固醇来源的胆汁酸前体 (A12)。
analysis_zh.results: 重新分析显示 VCAM1 在人类中呈保守上调 (log2FC +1.17, P = 0.023),在大鼠中 ICAM1 亦上调 (log2FC +0.32, padj = 0.016),且 FXR 未改变 (A6‐A7);感染大鼠肺部表现为 Nfkb1 持续抑制和 Slc10a2 下调 (P = 0.028) (A8);在 PUUV 感染的血管芯片中观察到 IL6 显著升高 (log2FC +1.22, P = 3.1×10−8) 且胆汁酸转运蛋白 ABCC3 丢失 (log2FC −1.44, P = 7.4×10−12) (A9);TGR5 在内皮细胞中检测不到 (A10)。FXR/TGR5 激动剂降低 NF‐κB 活性并减轻血管损伤 (A11),而 HTNV 诱导的 CH25H 上调阻断了 HMGCR 依赖的胆固醇合成 (A12)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本文提出一个统一的致病模型,将 汉坦病毒 引起的肠道菌群失调和胆固醇代谢受损与 FXR/TGR5 激动性胆汁酸的耗竭相联系,从而解除对内皮 NF‐κB 和单核细胞 NLRP3 炎症小体的抑制 (A13)。文中列出了针对多组学临床队列、体外受体检测和体内药理干预的分层、可检验的预测 (A14)。肠道微生物–胆汁酸–FXR/TGR5 轴被强调为 汉坦病毒 疾病的可再利用治疗靶点 (A15)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 作者承认缺乏将胆汁酸信号与 汉坦病毒 引起的血管损伤直接因果关联的证据 (A15);该工作是一项基于假设的综合,依赖于对已有数据集的重新分析,而非新的实验数据。

papers.title: t-PA/PAI-1 complex expression correlates with the severity in hantaan virus-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to investigate t-PAIC concentration changes across severity levels in HFRS patients and evaluate its value in predicting disease severity, providing a potential biomarker for HFRS severity assessment and monitoring. METHODS: t-PAIC levels were measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay in 156 HFRS patients and 37 healthy controls. Routine laboratory tests assessed WBC, PLT, Cr, UA, urea, HDL, ALB, APTT, and PT. HFRS-specific antibodies were detected using the colloidal gold method. Spearman correlation analysis evaluated associations between t-PAIC and clinical indices. Ordinal logistic regression identified risk factors linked to disease severity. ROC curve analysis assessed the predictive performance of t-PAIC for HFRS severity. RESULTS: t-PAIC levels progressively increased with HFRS severity, peaking in critically ill patients. t-PAIC showed significant positive correlations with leukocyte count (r = 0.6082; p < 0.01), Cr (r = 0.3567; p < 0.01), urea (r = 0.4376; p < 0.01), UA (r = 0.3201; p < 0.01), APTT (r = 0.6182; p < 0.01), and PT (r = 0.2997; p < 0.01), and significant inverse correlations with PLT (r = -0.6177; p < 0.01), HDL (r = -0.3074; p < 0.01), and ALB (r = -0.4790; p < 0.01). ROC analysis revealed t-PAIC had good predictive value for disease severity (AUC = 0.796, 95% CI: 0.724-0.867, p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: t-PAIC levels closely reflect HFRS severity and associated clinical features, including renal dysfunction and coagulation abnormalities, suggesting its potential as a biomarker for monitoring disease status.
papers.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

papers.title: Hantavirus: A Comprehensive Narrative Review of Virology, Epidemiology, Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations, Diagnostics, and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Hantaviruses are a genus of negative‐sense, single‐stranded, tri‐segmented RNA viruses that are distributed worldwide. They cause two severe zoonotic diseases in humans: haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), also known as hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Hantaviruses are primarily spread by inhaling aerosolised excreta from infected rodent reservoirs. Over 50 rodent species on six continents have been found to carry hantaviruses, with only one reported case of human‐to‐human transmission, involving the Andes virus (ANDV) in South America. HFRS is estimated to cause 100,000–150,000 cases worldwide annually, mainly in Asia and Europe. HPS/HCPS is far less common, with case fatality rates of 25%–40%, predominantly in the Americas. The pathogenesis of hantaviral disease is characterised by viral infection of endothelial cells, dysregulation of vascular permeability, and dysregulated innate and adaptive immune responses, leading to cytokine storm physiology. Diagnosis relies on enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)‐based serology and reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT‐PCR). Strain characterisation and outbreak investigations are increasingly being performed using next‐generation sequencing. No hantavirus species has a licenced vaccine outside of HTNV and SEOV, for which inactivated rodent‐brain‐derived vaccines remain in limited regional use in Korea and China. Regulatory‐agency‐approved antiviral therapy is similarly lacking worldwide, and management remains largely supportive. Ribavirin has shown benefit in reducing mortality and renal morbidity in HFRS when initiated early, but has not demonstrated efficacy in HPS/HCPS in controlled trials. Recent advancements include the development of monoclonal antibodies, candidate mRNA and subunit vaccines, and an improved understanding of the mechanisms of immune evasion. This review synthesises the latest information on hantavirus biology, clinical medicine and public health. This highlights the critical gaps that must be addressed to counter the growing threat posed by this pathogen in an era of climate change and global ecological transformation.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed negative‑sense RNA viruses, and rising ecological change heightens their public‑health relevance.
analysis.main_directions: The review covers the two major zoonoses (HFRS and HPS/HCPS), endothelial infection and immune dysregulation, and emerging therapeutic approaches such as monoclonal antibodies and vaccine candidates.
analysis.current_state: Transmission occurs mainly via inhalation of aerosolised rodent excreta; HFRS causes ~100‑150 k cases annually in Asia/Europe while HPS has 25‑40 % mortality in the Americas. papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andes Orthohantavirus (ANDV) carries case-fatality rates up to 40%; however, the innate immune determinants of disease severity remain poorly defined. Natural killer (NK) cells are central mediators of early antiviral immunity, but their landscape during the earliest phase of ANDV infection has not been characterized. Using multiparameter flow cytometry and unsupervised UMAP-based clustering in PBMCs from 13 HCPS patients stratified by severity and nine healthy donors, we show that severe HCPS is characterized by a coordinated disruption of the CD56dim NK cell compartment, encompassing reduced subset frequencies, specific reduction in the terminally differentiated NKG2C+CD57+ adaptive-like pool, and intrinsic impairment of IFN-γ production and degranulation, deficits that were absent in mild patients and persisted in part beyond clinical recovery. Furthermore, CD56dimCD16+ NK cell frequencies correlated negatively with viral load across all acute patients, independent of clinical severity. These findings establish severe HCPS not merely as a state of NK cell depletion, but as one of selective functional impairment of the most cytotoxically competent NK cell population during the critical early acute phase of ANDV infection.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS caused by ANDV has up to 40% fatality and innate immune drivers of severity are unclear. Methods: Flow cytometry and UMAP clustering were applied to PBMCs from 13 Chilean HCPS patients (by severity) and nine healthy donors. Contribution: The work reveals selective functional loss of the most cytotoxic NK cells early in ANDV infection, informing disease immunopathogenesis. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence; abstract only.

papers.title: Hantavirus Disease: A Comprehensive Narrative Review of Epidemiology, Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infection is a rodent-borne zoonotic disease of considerable public health importance. The disease is associated with a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations and continues to attract increasing attention because of its impact on human health and its evolving epidemiological patterns. This narrative review summarizes current knowledge regarding the epidemiology, virology, pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis, management, and prevention of hantavirus infection. A comprehensive literature search was conducted using major electronic databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Relevant peer-reviewed articles, reviews, clinical studies, surveillance reports, and guidelines were evaluated and synthesized to provide an updated overview of the subject. This narrative review discusses the interactions among environmental factors, rodent reservoirs, and human exposure that influence disease occurrence and transmission. Key aspects of disease pathogenesis, clinical presentation, diagnostic approaches, therapeutic considerations, and preventive measures are summarized. Current management strategies remain largely supportive, while ongoing research continues to explore novel diagnostic tools, therapeutic options, and preventive interventions. In conclusion, hantavirus infection remains an important public health concern. Continued efforts toward improved surveillance, timely diagnosis, enhanced research, and effective preventive strategies are essential for better disease control and improved patient outcomes.

papers.title: Differentiated Contact Tracing for Emerging Zoonotic Hantavirus and Ebolavirus Infections: Lessons from the 2026 Andes Virus (MV Hondius) and Bundibugyo Virus Outbreaks.
papers.abstract: In May 2026, two outbreaks occurred at once: an Andes virus outbreak aboard the MV Hondius expedition cruise ship (13 cases (12 laboratory-confirmed and 1 probable), 3 deaths, and more than 600 contacts traced across 32 countries and territories; passengers and crew from 23 countries; data as of 22 June 2026) and a Bundibugyo virus disease (BDBV) outbreak in Central Africa (more than 1000 laboratory-confirmed cases and more than 250 confirmed deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda; data as of 22 June 2026). The two pathogens diverge sharply in their transmission epidemiology. Aboard the MV Hondius, person-to-person transmission was sustained across three generations from a single index case, and one asymptomatic, PCR-positive contact later developed symptoms, indicating pre-symptomatic ANDV RNA detection, although the extent to which this corresponds to infectiousness and onward transmission remains uncertain. BDBV, on current evidence, has not been documented to sustain pre-symptomatic transmission as a major driver of its outbreaks, which allows for contact tracing of different timing and intensity. This Perspective draws together the epidemiological data from the MV Hondius outbreak, the endemic-region experience (Chile's 2021-2025 secondary attack rate of 5.7%; Argentina's 1996 El Bolsón and 2018 Epuyén outbreaks), the molecular pathogenesis, the diagnostic platforms, the therapeutic pipeline (favipiravir, tocilizumab, Icatibant) and the vaccine strategies (USAMRIID DNA vaccine, phase 1 completed). We set the contact-tracing and active-surveillance protocols applied to ANDV against the less stringent protocols that may suffice for BDBV.

papers.title: Person-to-Person Transmission of Andes Virus (ANDV): A Systematic Review of Transmission Dynamics, Viral Shedding, and Public Health Implications.
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus with well-documented evidence of person-to-person transmission. However, key parameters related to transmission timing, viral shedding, exposure contexts, and public health management remain incompletely defined. We conducted a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA 2020. MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception up to 14 May 2026. Eligible studies reported epidemiological, virological, clinical, or public health data relevant to ANDV infection, person-to-person transmission, viral shedding, and/or outbreak control. Thirty-three studies, including 17,204 individuals, 2221 laboratory-confirmed ANDV cases, and 135 documented secondary cases, were included. Person-to-person transmission was identified as a primary or co-occurring route in 20 papers. The median incubation period among ANDV cases was 20.8 days, and the median serial interval was 21.8 days (upper bounds near 40 days). Secondary attack rates were higher among sexual and other close contacts. ANDV RNA was consistently detected in blood and occasionally in saliva, respiratory secretions, urine, breast milk, and semen, although RNA detection alone does not necessarily imply infectious virus. Rare reports of culture-confirmed isolation of replication-competent virus support the biological plausibility of transmission via close mucosal or respiratory exposure. Unlike other hantaviruses, Andes virus can spread person to person through close contact, supporting prolonged monitoring and risk-stratified follow-up of high-risk contacts based on ANDV-specific epidemiological evidence. Possible recommendations, including post-discharge counselling regarding possible sexual transmission, remain provisional and require further evidence. Preparedness activities against outbreaks should also be implemented in non-endemic regions, while future research should prioritize prospective contact studies, standardized virological sampling, and genomic confirmation.
